strengths: Clear motivation for extending Nelson et al. (2022) to direct state-dependent rewards with well-articulated technical challenges
Stronger theoretical guarantees: high-probability bounds (vs. expectation-only), reward-model free, with fully adaptive HMM parameter estimation

Novel technical contributions including intermediate filtration U_t for managing measurability/belief trade-offs, L^2-based analysis for non-martingale terms, and staged elliptic potential lemma (Lemma E.6)
Comprehensive technical treatment with detailed proofs and systematic error decomposition (S'_diff, S'_belief, S'_eta)
Clear comparative analysis showing simplified model reduces to linear bandits while general model does not
weaknesses: Critical gap: No experimental validation despite promised 'version 2' - ICML typically requires experiments to validate theory and contextualize results

Suboptimal regret rates with unclear optimality: T^{7/8} for general model vs T^{3/4} for simplified model with T^{1/8} gap from staged approach; L^2-Markov bound may not be tight (√(1/δ_s) vs typical √ln(1/δ_s) dependency); only open problems stated regarding lower bounds
Restrictive assumptions: finite state/context spaces, full-rank emission matrix, invertible transition matrix, known H, exponentially fast forgetting of HMM

Dense presentation spanning 43 pages with complex staged algorithm, making main insights difficult to extract; Box A algorithm has intricate details and complex confidence bonus expressions; requires knowing horizon T in advance
Coupling to specific HMM estimation method (spectral): unknown threshold T_{B,M,ν} requires conservative initialization; robustness to model misspecification or HMM parameter error not analyzed
Missing practical considerations: computational complexity analysis, sensitivity to stage length parameter, failure mode analysis, implementation details, code

strengths: Technically rigorous analysis with detailed proofs and careful handling of complex state-belief-reward dependencies
Clear articulation of the distinction between belief-dependent (Nelson et al. 2022) vs. state-dependent reward models and why it matters
High-probability regret bounds (not just expectation), which are stronger guarantees than prior work
Novel staged LinUCB approach with explicit filtration construction to balance state estimation measurability constraints
Comprehensive appendices covering belief estimation, HMM forgetting properties, and complete proofs
weaknesses: Critical: Missing experimental validation. Paper explicitly states 'Numerical simulations will be provided in version 2' (Appendix F), indicating incomplete submission. Without experiments, cannot assess practicality, tightness of bounds, or algorithmic performance

Incremental theoretical improvements: T^{7/8} rate is not competitive with standard √T linear bandit results; authors acknowledge T^{1/8} loss comes from suboptimal L²-Markov bounds and identify improvement to T^{3/4} as an open problem, suggesting bound may be loose
No lower bounds provided: Cannot determine if T^{7/8} is optimal or an analytical artifact; missing information-theoretic characterization

Highly restrictive assumptions: Assumption 4.2 requires emission matrix full column rank with H < |X|, invertible M with positive entries, finite context space. Assumption 5.1 (exponentially fast forgetting) excludes many practical HMMs. Requires known horizon T for parameter selection

Limited practical motivation: No compelling real-world applications demonstrating when this specific model (rewards on states+contexts+actions) is preferred over simpler alternatives. No comparison of when state-dependent model is better than belief-dependent model

Algorithm practicality issues: Requires horizon T in advance, complex confidence bonuses ε_{t,a} with nested terms make implementation opaque, no computational complexity analysis, no guidance on hyperparameter selection

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy with limited intuition. Key distinction between models and algorithmic insights buried in technical details. Alignment step (Appendix C.2) for state labeling appears ad-hoc
Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (LinUCB, spectral HMM estimation, Nelson et al.'s L²-Markov bounds) without fundamental new insights

Incomplete related work: Brief treatment of Hong et al. (2020) and Galozy et al. (2025) without clear regret rate comparisons. Model comparison to belief-dependent case not entirely fair without empirical validation of which is more realistic

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: The paper articulates precisely why the belief-dependent model in Nelson et al. (2022) is a significant simplification, making a compelling case for studying state-dependent rewards in contextual bandits with HMM dynamics

Technically sophisticated analysis: The staged approach with carefully constructed filtration U_t elegantly addresses the tension between belief estimation and direct state dependencies; proper handling of HMM forgetting properties throughout

Improved guarantees over prior work: Provides high-probability (not expectation) bounds that are reward-model independent and don't require coverage assumptions; T^{3/4} for simplified model vs √T in expectation from Nelson et al.

Comprehensive treatment: Detailed proofs with non-trivial extensions of technical tools (e.g., elliptic potential lemma for staged updates in Lemma E.6); honest discussion of optimality gaps and limitations
Flexible and general framework: Belief estimation subroutine (Assumption 4.1) generalizes beyond specific implementations; concrete instantiations with spectral methods are well-established
Sound and thorough analysis: All proofs appear correct with careful treatment of complex dependencies; extensive appendices provide complete arguments and helper results
weaknesses: Missing experimental validation: No numerical simulations provided (promised for v2). Even synthetic experiments on simple problems would validate algorithms and reveal whether regret bounds are tight or loose

Suboptimal regret rates without clear improvement path: T^{7/8} and T^{3/4} are significantly worse than √T in standard settings. The L^2-Markov bottleneck is identified but no mechanism for improvement is proposed. No lower bounds provided to justify these rates

Limited novelty in individual components: Staged approach is straightforward; L^2-Markov inequality borrowed from Nelson et al.; spectral belief estimation from prior work. Main novelty is in combination rather than new techniques

Restrictive assumptions limiting applicability: Requires finite context sets, known H, invertible transition matrices, full-rank emission matrices. Unknown threshold T_{B,M,ν} complicates practical implementation. These constraints significantly limit when results apply
Suboptimal regret for simplified model: Even the belief-dependent model (which reduces to linear contextual bandits) only achieves T^{3/4} instead of √T, suggesting analysis may not be tight

Dense presentation with heavy notation: Section 3 (Challenges Overcome) is compressed and could benefit from more upfront intuition. Comparison to Nelson et al. needs clarification—comparing √T in expectation (their result) to T^{3/4} high-probability (this work) isn't straightforward

Missing practical implementation details: No guidance on choosing λ and ℓ without knowing T; confidence bonuses in Theorem 5.2 are complex; computational complexity not discussed; belief estimation threshold T_{B,M,ν} is unknown and complicated
